clue.text: Overheard, retailer is more repulsive

indicators.note: something overheard is caught by the ear, so the word is the one you hear rather than the one you see

blocks.note: a grocer is a retailer of food

explanation.surface: Some eavesdropped gossip reveals that a shopkeeper is even more disgusting.
explanation.definitionFit: Gross means disgusting, so its comparative form describes something even more disgusting.

clue.text: Very keen shooter — he's foremost in game

indicators.note: foremost picks out the letter at the very front of the word
in places the selected letter inside the following word

blocks.note: a gun is a shooter
Go is the Japanese board game; it holds the next piece
the first letter of he's

explanation.surface: An eager marksman leads the way when it comes to hunting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' suggests hunted animals for the shooter, but it is the board game Go.
explanation.definitionFit: Gung-ho describes someone overly enthusiastic and eager, especially for a fight.

clue.text: Abroad, place for spending

blocks.note: out of the country, away
to lay something is to place it

explanation.surface: A holiday spot overseas where one can splash out.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlay is an amount of money spent, so it is a noun meaning expenditure.

clue.text: Yorkshire town accepting large fruit — no good if past this?

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the town admits a letter inside it

blocks.note: Selby is a market town in North Yorkshire
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing
a date is the fruit of the date palm

explanation.surface: A northern town takes delivery of big fruit that may be going off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description rather than a synonym, flagged by the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A sell-by date is printed on food packaging, and goods beyond it should no longer be sold or may be spoiled.

clue.text: What unrepentant one will do with sticky stuff

definitions.note: read as RE-SIN, to sin again

blocks.note: first meaning, split as two parts: to sin once more
second meaning: the gummy substance from trees

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as re-sin: someone who does not repent will sin again.
explanation.definitionFit: Resin is a viscous sap exuded by pine and other trees, and broken up it reads as committing a sin again.

clue.text: Old tragedian initially greeting play

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
the first letter of tragedian
a common greeting

explanation.surface: A veteran tragic actor's first words of welcome open a stage performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy about the Moor of Venice is a famous example of a play.

clue.text: Band of gold artist put round box

indicators.note: put round means placed on either side of, so the outer pieces surround another

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a chest is a large box
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: A gold ring wrapped around a jewellery box by a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: The gold and the artist sit either side of the box.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large group of musicians, and band is a general word for such a group.

clue.text: Fried food, but not the first fruit

indicators.note: but not the first tells you to drop the opening letter of the word before

blocks.note: chips are fried potatoes

explanation.surface: Something from the deep fryer that is not, after all, the first piece of fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Hips are the red berries left on rose bushes after flowering, also called rosehips.

clue.text: Tough pasture north of the railway

blocks.note: a lea is a meadow
taken as written
RY is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A rough field lying just above the train line.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, north of means placed above, so the meadow comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Leathery means hard and tough like leather, as of skin or overcooked meat.

clue.text: Dismissed correctly, without qualification

blocks.note: a batsman who is dismissed is out
right means correctly, as in 'guess right'

explanation.surface: A batsman was given out fairly, with no doubts about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Outright means completely and unreservedly, so it applies with no conditions or reservations attached.

clue.text: African province once concerned with delivery?

blocks.note: first meaning: a former province of South Africa
second meaning: relating to birth, the delivery of a baby

explanation.walkthrough: Delivery suggests post or parcels; the question mark flags that it means childbirth here.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective natal relates to birth, and Natal was also the name of a South African province until 1994.

clue.text: I'm obsequious chap, stony broke

definitions.note: the answer describes itself in the first person

indicators.note: something broke has been smashed into pieces, so these letters are reassembled in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words together

explanation.surface: A fawning man confesses his servility, adding that he is completely penniless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony broke' reads as one phrase meaning penniless, but broke is the anagram signal working on the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sycophant is a toady who flatters the powerful, so he could truthfully say he is servile and fawning.

clue.text: Boss with old motor for heavy metal fan

blocks.note: the head is the person in charge
in British slang a banger is a battered old car

explanation.surface: A manager who drives a clapped-out car turns out to love loud rock music.
explanation.definitionFit: Headbangers are rock fans who shake their heads violently in time to the music at concerts.

clue.text: Asian commitment, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, so the word is chosen for its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a tie is something that binds you, an obligation

explanation.surface: Someone's pledge to a person from Asia, as rumour has it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thai is a person from Thailand, a country in Southeast Asia, so the word works as a noun or adjective.

clue.text: Chelsea neighbour makes former mayor serenade knight

blocks.note: Ken Livingstone was the first Mayor of London
to serenade someone is to sing to them
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: An ex-mayor croons a love song to a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea may suggest the football club, but it is the London district, and Kensington is the area next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Kensington is a district of west London bordering Chelsea, both part of one borough.

clue.text: Practical direction at end of flight

blocks.note: first meaning: sensible and realistic
second meaning, read literally: where an aircraft heads as it lands

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the idiom word by word, as a heading for an aircraft coming in to land.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a sensible, unpretentious person, and literally names the way a plane goes when it comes in to land.

clue.text: Wood turned with spanner somewhere in Surrey

indicators.note: turned means facing the opposite way, so the tree's name is read from the end

blocks.note: yew is a tree and its timber
a bridge spans a river or gap

explanation.surface: Timber shaped on a lathe using a wrench, somewhere in the Home Counties.
explanation.walkthrough: Spanner looks like a tool but means something that spans. Surrey is a county just south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Weybridge is a town in the county of Surrey, so it is one location within it.

clue.text: The Guardian somehow ignoring final boy or girl

indicators.note: somehow suggests things done in some unknown way, so the letters are rearranged
ignoring final means the ending is left out, so the closing letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; its last three letters go
Ian is a boy's name, removed from the end

explanation.surface: The newspaper somehow overlooks the end result of whether a baby is a boy or girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boy or girl' looks like the definition, but the boy's name is what comes off the end of the newspaper's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A daughter is a female child, and girl is commonly used for one's own daughter.

clue.text: Dicky bird let fluid escape? Let fluid escape!

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the word it qualifies is disordered

blocks.note: the letters of the word
to bleed is to lose blood, a fluid

explanation.surface: A sick bird that may or may not have dripped, and yes, it did.
explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase serves twice: with a question mark as a cryptic hint at bled, then plainly as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To dribble is to let liquid trickle out slowly, as from the mouth.

clue.text: What things might come to scenic mountain route?

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for a sorry state of affairs, as in 'things have come to...'
second meaning, read literally: an attractive way through mountains

explanation.surface: A traveller wonders where a beautiful road through the hills might lead.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'things have come to a pretty pass' means matters have got bad, and a pass is a route through mountains.

clue.text: Check polish once more

blocks.note: first meaning: to repel or snub
second meaning: buff again

explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer as re-buff, buffing a surface again.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuff is to check or repel an advance, and to buff is to polish, so a second buffing is a re-buff.

clue.text: Paddy is moderate

blocks.note: first meaning: a paddy is British slang for a fit of anger
second meaning: to soften or tone down

explanation.surface: A man called Paddy is a calm and reasonable fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like a name but means a tantrum, and moderate is a verb, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A temper is an outburst of rage, and to temper something is to soften or restrain it.

clue.text: Trap one in desert

blocks.note: trap and gob are both slang for the mouth
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Setting a snare for someone out in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: Trap looks like a verb but is the noun, slang for the mouth, as in 'shut your trap'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gobi is the large desert spanning northern China and southern Mongolia.

clue.text: A family member in the country ain't crude

indicators.note: crude means rough and unrefined, so the word it describes is reshaped into new order
in places one set of letters inside the other word

blocks.note: a country in southern Europe; the letters split around the inserted piece
the letters of the word, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A relative complains, in coarse slang, that something is not so in their homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The country' is vague on purpose; crossings settle Greece, and the rearranged ain't sits after its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-niece is the granddaughter of one's brother or sister, so she is a relative.

clue.text: Pungent article found by police? That's about right

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the police abbreviation is wrapped around a letter

blocks.note: the indefinite article
the Criminal Investigation Department of British police; it holds the next piece
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Detectives come across a strong-smelling item, and it is just about correct.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrid describes a sharp, bitter smell or taste, as of smoke.

clue.text: Characters from Capri on another island

indicators.note: characters from means some of the letters taken from the words that follow, in a run

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of one word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: People from one Italian island visit a different island.
explanation.walkthrough: Capri is an obvious island, which makes it look like the definition; it is just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland, known for its abbey.

clue.text: Story about nobleman beginning to refuse unreasonable demand

indicators.note: beginning to picks out the opening letter of the following word
about means around, so the story wraps itself round another word

blocks.note: a tale is a story; it opens to hold the next piece
a lord is a nobleman
the first letter of refuse

explanation.surface: A tale of an aristocrat who starts by turning down an excessive request.
explanation.walkthrough: The nobleman goes inside the story just before its last letter, and the starting letter of refuse is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall order is an idiom for a task or request that is very hard to fulfil.

clue.text: So short politician provides clobber

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the word before it loses its last letter

blocks.note: thus means so, in that way
MP stands for Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A diminutive MP turns out to be supplying the clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Clobber is British slang for clothes, but here it is the verb meaning to hit hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To clobber someone is to strike them heavily, which is what a thump is.

clue.text: Bureaucracy involving deep art

indicators.note: involving in its old sense of entangling or twisting together signals the letters get mixed up

blocks.note: the letters of both words together

explanation.surface: Official paperwork that somehow requires profound artistic skill.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is the idiom for excessive official rules and procedures, named after the ribbon once used to tie up documents.

clue.text: Teacher with English class not entirely doomed

indicators.note: not entirely means incomplete, so the word before it loses its final letter

blocks.note: a don is a university teacher
standard abbreviation for English
a form is a class in a British school

explanation.surface: A lecturer and an English group who are not quite finished off.
explanation.definitionFit: Done for is an informal phrase meaning ruined or beyond saving.
